cards.anchor: Preserve the bounded outcome: three depth-vial attenuations with normalized spread at most 4 percent at second-120 sampling, reducing stirring time if feasible. One stipulated 300 rpm, 60-second trial achieved approximately 2.4 percent; reliable repetition remains hypothetical.
cards.burden: Two lower-speed repetitions offer limited reliability evidence. Four fresh trials including speed comparators consume session capacity. Report every raw vial reading, sampling order, duration and target failure; unknown preferred-rule duration prevents a baseline time-saving claim.
cards.construction: Hypothesis: timed bulk rotation can achieve the sample proxy without optical stability governing duration. Use fresh rinsed recipes of 150 mL water and 0.30 mL dye. Command 300 rpm for exactly 60 seconds, then no restart before sampling at second 120. Side checks every five seconds have logging authority only. Hold bottle, camera, addition location and references fixed; alternate depth order. Use the spill tray and stop if liquid escapes.
cards.defeat: Repeated final spread above 4 percent defeats reliable success for this recipe and schedule. Strong sampling-order dependence challenges interpretation of apparent success. Neither result establishes 900 rpm necessity.
cards.mutation: Replace sustained high-speed optical-feedback stopping with a fixed lower-speed dose and independent final-vial acceptance.
cards.prediction_candidate: Hypothesis predicts both fresh 300 rpm repetitions meet the final-vial target even when moving side checks fail it. Successful repetitions would strengthen bounded feasibility without establishing general sufficiency.
cards.prediction_rival: Exceptional or sampling-mediated prior success predicts repeat target failures or systematic sampling-order dependence. A small successful sample cannot exclude rare failure.
cards.probe: Allocate trials 1-4 to two fixed-duration 300/900 rpm pairs: first pair 300 then 900, second pair 900 then 300. Each run stirs 60 seconds and rests 60 seconds before second-120 sampling; withdraw 1 mL at 10, 28 and 45 mm within ten seconds. The two 300 runs test repetition; their matched 900 partners support the second card’s temporal comparison. Use water-only/common-aliquot references and report normalized spreads.
cards.rival: The prior lower-speed success was exceptional, or sampling disturbance masked gradients; timed 300 rpm does not reliably meet the target.
unknowns: No concentration calibration or independent tachometer; common-aliquot agreement is repeatability only.
Sampling can redistribute dye; only two lower-speed repetitions constrain reliability.
Other recipes, scales and continuous operation are untested; this synthetic proxy implies no real chemical or human benefit.

cards.anchor: Maintain the same independent final-vial spread target at second 120 while testing whether optical feedback adds stirring after the outcome is achievable. Future 900 rpm timer success and any time savings remain hypotheses.
cards.burden: Use the remaining two trials for feedback comparison, bringing the integrated schedule to six within 90 minutes. A single feedback pair and two fixed-speed pairs support only bounded evidence. Manual image readings and speck counts impose recording work.
cards.construction: Hypothesis: commanded agitation renews optical disturbance, and failed checks return further agitation commands. In trials 5-6, compare fresh 900 rpm recipes: predetermined stop at 60 seconds with the preferred rule logged in shadow mode, then enabled rule stopping after three successive five-second checks at most 4 percent, capped at second 105. Hold recipe, references, addition location and camera fixed; sample at second 120 and alternate depth order. Record side spread, commanded duration, depression and speck frames. Keep the spill tray and stop escaping liquid.
cards.defeat: Timer target failure with enabled target success defeats the proposed outcome-preserving severance in this pair. Both failures leave the mechanism unresolved. No extra enabled stirring, or no duration reduction with both succeeding, defeats demonstrated feedback cost here. Persistent post-stop optical spread weakens disturbance renewal, without identifying its cause.
cards.mutation: Sever optical spread’s command link to stirring while retaining shadow decisions; use matched externally commanded cessation to examine the reversed agitation-to-image arrow.
cards.prediction_candidate: If 60 seconds suffices and agitation renews disturbances, shadow checks may continue to fail while timer and enabled trials both meet final-vial targets; enabled stirring would last longer. In trials 1-4, 900 rpm may show greater moving-frame disturbance and a prompt post-stop decline despite successful vials. These outcomes support the proposed effects conditionally, without proving bubbles or an operating loop.
cards.prediction_rival: Unresolved gradients predict timer failure with longer enabled success. Genuine gradients may retain spread after stopping and accompany vial failure; persistent optical artifacts may retain side spread despite successful vials. These alternatives do not predict a reliably cessation-sensitive renewal effect.
cards.probe: Compare trials 5-6 durations, shadow decisions and final vials. Reuse trials 1-4 for matched moving and five-second post-stop images with equal 60-second quiet intervals and reversed speed order. Record each cessation time: unequal quiet intervals in the feedback pair confound attribution of vial differences solely to additional stirring. Report all outcomes and failures.
cards.rival: Actual unresolved dye gradients cause optical spread, and additional agitation helps redistribution; alternatively persistent optical artifacts explain image differences without agitation-renewed feedback.
unknowns: Specks do not identify bubbles; bubble fraction and absolute concentration cannot be measured with supplied resources.
Rapid image changes can reflect surface shape or settling; they cannot prove uniformity before the quiet interval.
No matched observed 900 rpm final vials or established rule-driven prolongation; nominal speed, sampling disturbance, quiet-time differences and limited replication constrain causal attribution.
